report.tagline: An Estonian ride-hailing and delivery app that beats Uber on price by taking a smaller cut from drivers.
report.simpleSummary: Bolt is an app for booking a car ride, like Uber. You enter where you are going, see a price, and a driver picks you up. It is often a bit cheaper than Uber because Bolt keeps a smaller share of each fare and runs a very lean company. In many cities the same app also rents e-scooters and e-bikes and delivers food and groceries.

overview.whatItDoes: Bolt matches riders with drivers who use their own or rented cars, and takes a commission on each trip. It also offers scooters and e-bikes, Bolt Food, Bolt Market grocery delivery, Bolt Drive car-sharing and Bolt Business for companies. Ride-hailing is about four fifths of revenue.
howItWorks: Rider opens the app, enters a destination and picks a car type such as Bolt, Comfort, XL or Green (electric).
Bolt shows an upfront price, which is often below Uber in the same city.
A nearby driver accepts and the rider tracks the car on a map.
Payment is by card or, in many markets, cash.
Bolt keeps a commission, which it says is under 20% in many markets, and pays the rest to the driver.
The same app unlocks scooters and e-bikes or orders food in cities where those run.
overview.valueProposition: For riders: rides that are usually cheaper than Uber. For drivers: a smaller commission, so more of each fare stays with them. For cities: one app that mixes cars, scooters and bikes.

businessModel.summary: Bolt makes money by taking a cut of every ride and delivery. Its whole plan is to have lower costs than Uber, so it can charge drivers less and riders less and still make a small profit.

revenueStreams.detail: A share of each fare, the biggest stream at about 82% of revenue in 2024.
Restaurants and shops pay a share, and customers pay a delivery fee on Bolt Food and Bolt Market.
Hourly and daily rental fees on Bolt Drive.
Rides for companies, sometimes with a service fee.

businessModel.pricing: Dynamic upfront pricing that varies by city and demand. Not published as a fixed rate card. Commission to drivers is advertised as under 20% in many markets.
costDrivers: Driver bonuses and rider discounts to win share
Insurance and licensing, which is high in the UK
Scooter and e-bike hardware, charging and repairs
Courier pay for food and grocery
Engineering, kept small compared with Uber
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a £15 London ride. If Bolt keeps about 20%, it earns about £3. The driver keeps about £12, more than they would on Uber. From the £3, Bolt pays card fees, insurance-related costs, support and promos. Across the whole company in 2025, Bolt kept about €19.5 million of operating profit on €2.27 billion of revenue, under 1%. So Bolt breaks even only by spending far less per ride on staff and marketing than Uber.

howTheyGetUsers: Lower prices that win app comparisons
Driver sign-up bonuses that bring supply first
Launching fast in new cities, hundreds of them in 2025
Scooters on the street act as free ads
whatBringsUsersBack: Habit of checking Bolt for a cheaper price
growth.moat: Bolt's moat is its low cost base. It runs with far fewer staff per ride than Uber, so it can survive on a smaller commission. It is also number one in more than 20 countries, mostly in Eastern Europe and Africa, where local density keeps wait times short.

improvementIdeas.idea: Price and wait time shown together with a guarantee
improvementIdeas.problem: Riders pick Uber when Bolt's wait is unclear.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: A pickup time promise with a credit if missed builds trust in Bolt's lower price.

improvementIdeas.problem: Driver cancels are a top complaint.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Fewer cancels and faster completed trips.

improvementIdeas.idea: Human support for safety and payment disputes
improvementIdeas.problem: Automated support frustrates users after a bad trip.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Higher trust and fewer bad reviews.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Support satisfaction score and rider retention after a ticket

improvementIdeas.problem: Bolt earns less from higher-value business trips.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: More steady weekday demand at higher fares.

pmLessons: A low price is only a strategy if your costs are lower too; Bolt proves this by running lean.
In ride-hailing, supply comes first: a lower commission to drivers was Bolt's way into Uber's markets.
Bundling several products in one app can raise use per customer, but each product must not drain profit.
Profit can be one bad quarter away when margins are under 1%, so guardrail metrics matter.

interviewQuestions.question: How would Bolt win more share from Uber in London?
interviewQuestions.hint: Split riders by trip type and price sensitivity. Look at driver supply at peak. Pick one segment, like students or night trips, and a metric.

interviewQuestions.question: Bolt's commission is lower than Uber's. Should it raise it?
interviewQuestions.hint: Model driver churn, wait times and rider prices. Test in one city. Watch guardrails like wait time.

interviewQuestions.question: Bolt wants to grow Bolt Food. Is that a good idea?
interviewQuestions.hint: Check overlap with riders, courier sharing, and margin. Compare with focusing on rides.

interviewQuestions.question: Rider retention in month two dropped. How do you investigate?
interviewQuestions.hint: Cohort by city and channel, check promos ending, wait times, price win rate and app bugs.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature to make riders feel safer on Bolt at night.
interviewQuestions.hint: List the fears, pick one, propose a feature like a verified pickup PIN, and a safety metric.

assumptions: The £15 London ride example uses Bolt's advertised commission of under 20% and is an illustration.
Uber's London commission of about 25% is a widely reported figure, not from Uber's filings.
Customer and partner counts are Sacra estimates.
Completed trips per week as north star is our choice; Bolt has not published its internal metric.
